source_text:
Consequens vero mihi videtur, ut quod est simplex, etiam sit immortale. Et quo pacto illud, ausculta: Nihil eorum quae sunt, seipsum corrumpit; alioquin enim ne initio quidem constitisset. Quae autem corrumpuntur, ex contrariis corrumpuntur. Nam omne quod corrumpitur, dissolvitur: quod dissolvitur, compositum est: at compositum, multarum est partium: quod ex partibus constat, ex iis scilicet constat differentibus: quod vero differens est; idem non est: Quamobrem cum simplex sit Anima, neque ex pluribus partibus constet; quia nec composita est, nec dissolvi potest: sequitur eam incorruptibilem, et immortalem esse.

Praeterea, quidquid alieno cietur motu, nec ex se ipso, sed ex eo, a quo movetur, vivendi habet facultatem; illud tam diu permanet, quod ab illa intrinsecus operante vi conservatur: at ubi ea cessaverit, et ipsum quod ab ea movebatur, desinat necesse est. Quare cum Anima a seipsa moveatur, nunquam esse desinit. Haec enim ita se consequuntur, ut quod a seipso movetur, semper moveatur, quod semper movetur, nunquam deficit: quod nunquam deficit, fine caret: quod finis est expers, non corrumpitur: quod non corrumpitur, est immortale. Ergo si Anima a se ipsa movetur, ut superius demonstratum est; erit igitur ex vi iam propositae ratiocinationis, incorruptibilis et immortalis.

Praeterea, quodcunque a proprio malo non corrumpitur, corrumpi non potest: malum autem bono contrarium est; ideo et illius corrumpendi vim habet. Non enim aliud est corporis malum, quam passio, morbus, et mors; sicut e contra virtus eius est, pulchritudo, vita, sanitas, et firma constitutio. Si igitur Anima a suo malo non corrumpitur; malum autem Animae, est metus, intemperantia, invidia, et similia: quae tamen omnia vivendi ac movendi facultatem ipsi non auferunt: Anima ergo est immortalis.
thought_title: The soul is shown to be immortal because it is simple and self-moving
orientation: Gregory continues the treatise by arguing that the soul's simplicity entails its immortality, then adds proofs from self-motion and the nature of evil.
pass_a_gloss: It follows next to me that what is simple is also immortal. And how that is so, listen: Nothing of those things that exist corrupts itself; for otherwise it would not have been constituted even at the beginning. But things that are corrupted are corrupted by contraries. For every thing that is corrupted is dissolved; what is dissolved is composite; but a composite thing consists of many parts; what stands from parts stands from those different parts; what is different is not the same. Therefore since the soul is simple, and does not consist of many parts; because it is neither composite nor able to be dissolved; it follows that it is incorruptible and immortal. Moreover, whatever is moved by an alien motion has the power of living not from itself but from that by which it is moved; that thing lasts as long as it is preserved by that force operating intrinsically; but where that force has ceased, it is necessary that even what was moved by it also ceases. Therefore since the soul is moved by itself, it never ceases to be. For these things follow in such a way that what is moved by itself is always moved; what is always moved never fails; what never fails lacks an end; what lacks an end is not corrupted; what is not corrupted is immortal. Therefore if the soul is moved by itself, as was demonstrated above; it will therefore be incorruptible and immortal from the force of the reasoning already proposed. Moreover, whatever is not corrupted by its own evil cannot be corrupted: but evil is contrary to good; therefore it also has the power of corrupting it. For there is no other evil of body than passion, sickness, and death; just as on the contrary its good is beauty, life, health, and firm constitution. If therefore the soul is not corrupted by its own evil; but the evil of the soul is fear, intemperance, envy, and similar things: which however do not all take away the power of living and moving from it: therefore the soul is immortal.

choices.why: Reflexive destruction; the glossary bans 'destroys itself' but 'corrupts itself' matches the lemma.
Standard philosophical phrase; 'contraries' keeps the technical sense.

choices.english: is moved by an alien motion
choices.why: 'Alien' captures 'alieno' as 'belonging to another' without modern 'external'.
Keeps the adverbial force of 'intrinsecus' modifying the participle.

choices.english: but evil is contrary to good
choices.why: Direct statement of the logical relation used in the argument.
rejected: evil is the contrary of good

choices.why: Three bodily evils listed; 'passion' covers suffering/affection.

pass_b_english: It follows that what is simple is also immortal. Here is how it works: nothing that exists corrupts itself; otherwise it would never have been constituted in the first place. Things that are corrupted are corrupted by contraries. For everything that is corrupted is dissolved; what is dissolved is composite; what is composite consists of many parts; what consists of parts consists specifically of different parts; and what is different is not the same. Therefore, since the soul is simple and does not consist of many parts — because it is neither composite nor capable of being dissolved — it follows that it is incorruptible and immortal.

Furthermore, whatever is moved by an alien motion does not have the power to live from itself, but from that by which it is moved; it endures as long as it is preserved by the force operating intrinsically from that source. But when that force ceases, the thing moved by it must also cease. Therefore, since the soul is moved by itself, it never ceases to be. These steps follow one another: what is moved by itself is always moved; what is always moved never fails; what never fails lacks an end; what lacks an end is not corrupted; what is not corrupted is immortal. So if the soul is moved by itself, as has been demonstrated above, it will be incorruptible and immortal by the force of the reasoning already proposed.

Moreover, whatever is not corrupted by its own evil cannot be corrupted at all. Evil is contrary to good, and therefore has the power to corrupt it. For the evil of a body is nothing other than passion, sickness, and death; whereas its good, on the contrary, is beauty, life, health, and firm constitution. If the soul is not corrupted by its own evil — and the evil of the soul is fear, intemperance, envy, and the like — yet none of these take away its power to live and move; therefore the soul is immortal.
